description: Olá! Sou Luciano Tomé, de São Paulo, Brasil. Tenho mais de 20 anos de experiência em TI, com atuação em desenvolvimento de software, Unix/Linux, infraestrutura, DevOps, Cloud, IA e Agentic AI. Estou formando a equipe RUBIKS3 para o NASA Space Apps Challenge. Buscamos pessoas criativas e colaborativas com interesse em IA, Data Science, desenvolvimento, UX/UI, ciência e pesquisa. Estudantes e profissionais são bem-vindos.

We developed Orbit Pulse and Orbit Health, an offline-first health monitoring MVP designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. Orbit Pulse is an ESP32-based wearable prototype that collects physiological data such as heart rate, oxygen saturation, and body temperature, while also allowing astronauts to report mood, stress, fatigue, loneliness, sleep quality, and sleep duration.

The data is transmitted to Orbit Health, a local software platform built with FastAPI and SQLite. Orbit Health stores the information, tracks longitudinal trends, runs a deterministic risk engine, and classifies the astronaut’s condition as NOMINAL, WATCH, ACTION, or URGENT. It also provides explainable findings, recommended next actions, reaction-time testing, and operational history.

Our solution addresses the challenge by helping astronauts identify health changes early and act on them even without continuous communication with Earth. The next stage of the MVP is integrating a small local LLM to generate clear, protocol-constrained explanations and action suggestions based on the collected data.
details:
Orbit Health is an offline-first astronaut health monitoring and decision-support MVP designed for long-duration space missions. The project is composed of two integrated systems: Orbit Pulse, an ESP32-based wearable prototype, and Orbit Health, a local software platform that receives, stores, analyzes, and presents the astronaut’s health data.

Orbit Pulse collects physiological measurements such as heart rate, oxygen saturation, and body temperature. It also allows the astronaut to complete a short daily behavioral and recovery questionnaire covering mood, stress, fatigue, loneliness, sleep quality, and sleep duration. The device includes an OLED display, navigation buttons, status LEDs, a buzzer, and an emergency button. For the MVP, the wearable is developed and tested using the Wokwi ESP32 simulator.

The ESP32 transmits structured JSON events over Wi-Fi to Orbit Health. Each event receives a unique identifier, and questionnaire responses are grouped into unique sessions. A persistent NVS queue allows events to remain stored locally when communication is temporarily unavailable and be transmitted later.

Orbit Health runs locally and was developed using Python, FastAPI, SQLite, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The backend receives wearable events, validates them, stores them in the local SQLite database, and maintains longitudinal health history. The system also includes a reaction-time test that provides additional information about vigilance and operational performance.

A deterministic Risk Engine evaluates current measurements, questionnaire responses, recent trends, sensor quality, and performance indicators. It classifies the astronaut’s current state as NOMINAL, WATCH, ACTION, or URGENT. The dashboard explains why the state was assigned and provides predefined next actions instead of relying on an unexplained black-box result.

The system has already been tested end-to-end. Orbit Pulse can transmit sensor measurements and a complete six-question wearable session to Orbit Health. The information is persisted in SQLite, reconstructed as a complete session, processed by the Risk Engine, and displayed in the dashboard together with the resulting health state, score, findings, recommended actions, and operational history.

One of the main design decisions was to make the architecture offline-first. Core functions do not require continuous Internet or Earth connectivity. Data collection, local storage, risk assessment, historical analysis, and the dashboard can all operate on an onboard or edge computer.

Another important design decision was to combine objective sensor data with subjective self-reported information. A physiological measurement alone may not show the full operational condition of a crew member. By combining sensor measurements, sleep, stress, fatigue, mood, isolation, reaction time, and longitudinal trends, the system can provide a broader view of changes over time.

The next stage of the MVP is the integration of a small local Large Language Model with a few billion parameters. The LLM will not replace the deterministic Risk Engine or independently determine the astronaut’s medical condition. Instead, it will receive structured data from Orbit Health and help summarize trends, explain findings in natural language, and generate clearer action suggestions.

To reduce the risk of unrestricted AI output, the planned architecture will constrain the model using structured JSON output, predefined action allowlists, and validation rules. The Risk Engine will remain responsible for the primary state classification, while the local LLM will act as an explainability and communication layer.

The intended impact of Orbit Health is to demonstrate how astronauts could receive understandable and actionable health information locally during long-duration missions, especially when communication with Earth is delayed or unavailable. The MVP is an educational decision-support prototype and is not a certified medical device. It is intended to demonstrate a technical architecture that could later be mapped to validated mission medical requirements and protocols.
